native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is significantly stronger, more positive, and more productive in developing countries (Lower-Middle-Income Countries, LMC) than in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). In per-capita investment terms, increasing education expenditure is strongly and positively correlated with per capita GDP growth in developing countries (r = +0.9724, slope = +54.31), whereas in Sub-Saharan Africa the relationship is attenuated or negative (r = -0.9278). In expenditure share elasticity models, developing countries display significantly higher responsiveness (elasticity = -2.0712 vs -0.3423, interaction p = 0.001), underpinned by higher secondary school enrollment attainment (64.53% vs 43.37%). Accounting for autoregression and trade proxies, education expenditure fuels sustained productivity and output growth in developing countries, whereas its economic dividend is constrained in Sub-Saharan Africa.
native_result.WorkflowB: Reshaped World Bank panel dataset (1975-2015) to long format; computed per-capita education investment; conducted bivariate correlation and elasticity regressions for overlapping period (2011-2015); fitted interactive pooled OLS model; evaluated dynamic autoregressive specifications controlling for trade shocks (exports) and human capital proxies (secondary school enrollment).
